This paper introduces GLVD, a hybrid method for 3D face reconstruction from few-shot images. It extends Learned Vertex Descent (LVD) by integrating per-vertex neural field optimization with global structural guidance from dynamically predicted 3D keypoints.

Initially, the paper received mixed ratings. The primary concerns raised by reviewers included: limited technical novelty beyond LVD, insufficient quality of 3D representation capability, and a lack of clear method descriptions and implementation details. During the rebuttal and discussion period, the authors’ response successfully addressed most of the reviewers’ concerns, and the paper ultimately received 3 "Borderline Accept" ratings and 1 "Accept" rating.

After considering the paper, the reviews, and the rebuttal, the Area Chair believes this work meets the standards of NeurIPS. Accordingly, the Area Chair recommends acceptance. The authors are requested to revise the paper by addressing the reviewers’ comments in preparation for the camera-ready version.
We thank the reviewer for their positive assessment. We will highlight the distinctions from LVD in the final version.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful follow-up and for acknowledging the clarifications and new ablation study. We appreciate your suggestions.

---

We do not currently provide quantitative ablations comparing supervision on the full displacement matrix versus only the diagonal. As outlined in our response to Reviewer 5vBD, we implemented single-vertex distance prediction by introducing identity information in the form of Fourier features. Due to time constraints, we are unable to include the corresponding quantitative evaluations at this stage, but we will incorporate them in the final version of the manuscript.


(1) The decoder heads $g_v$ and $g_k$ are applied independently to each vertex, predicting displacements to all possible ground-truth vertices. That is, for each vertex, a displacement is computed with respect to every ground-truth vertex. To form the full displacement matrix, we query all points at test time. However, during training, we do not supervise the full matrix directly. Instead, the loss is computed individually for each query point. The final update is obtained by extracting the diagonal, which corresponds to the displacement of each query point to its designated target vertex.

(2) We apologize for the confusion. The keypoints are fixed and consistent across all training samples. The phrase "for each mesh" refers to each training sample, but the same set of selected keypoints is used throughout.  

(3) To clarify, the selected keypoints are **not** chosen randomly. They are manually selected based on semantic relevance to the task and remain fixed during training and testing.  Figure 1 in the supplementary material provides visual examples of the ablated keypoints that are quantitatively evaluated in Table 2 of the main manuscript. The red points shown in the supplementary video are indeed the actual selected keypoints, and we will update the caption and main text to make this explicit.

We thank the reviewer for their helpful comments and suggestions.

---



(1) We will update Figure 2 to include the RGB visualization of the PCA projection of the feature maps from the face.

(2) While this formulation is valid, we found that performance improved when regressing distances to all vertices and then selecting the output corresponding to the queried vertex. Specifically, the function $g_v$ maps the input feature vector to an output of size $\mathbb{R}^{3 \times N}$, where $N$ is the number of vertices. This corresponds to the full set of predicted vertex positions $\hat{\mathbf{V}} = [\hat{\mathbf{v}}_1, \dots, \hat{\mathbf{v}}_N]$.

Both $g_k$ and $g_v$ are implemented as 3-layer MLPs. We will emphasize this more clearly and include it in the main text. Both decoders are applied iteratively until convergence.

(3) While it is possible to directly predict the position of a specific vertex $\mathbf{v}_i$, doing so requires injecting information about which query point is being referred to. This can be implemented in several ways.

In our case, we experimented with using an identity feature vector for each query point. At test time, the process works as follows: we randomly sample $N$ vertices and assign each one a unique target ID. For each vertex, we concatenate its identity feature to the input, allowing the decoder head to infer which $\mathbf{v}_i$ to predict. We construct this identity feature by computing a Fourier feature embedding [9] of the vertex’s 3D coordinates in the original face template. We empirically found it to be more stable and to yield better results by encoding trajectories implicitly: for each query point, we predict displacements toward all possible target vertices, and then select the desired target vertex ID at test time.

A more detailed description of this process will be included in the main text.

---

# References

[9] Tancik, Matthew, et al. "Fourier features let networks learn high frequency functions in low dimensional domains." Advances in neural information processing systems 33 (2020): 7537-7547.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you very much for your evaluation of our paper. We are glad you found it easy to follow.

---

**AC note:** We appreciate the reviewer bringing this to the AC’s attention. While the visual style and figure layout in Figures 4, 5, and Supplementary Figure 6 are indeed similar to those in [1], this was done intentionally to facilitate a clear side-by-side comparison with a recent state-of-the-art method. Our goal was to ensure a fair and consistent visual analysis for readers. No identifying information was included in the submission, and we have carefully followed the double-blind review policy throughout.

---

## Novelty

We thank the reviewer for their comments and would like to respectfully clarify that characterizing our method as merely adding a face-landmark branch on top of LVD is an oversimplification.
While our work builds upon the iterative refinement principle of LVD, our formulation introduces several key innovations that fundamentally distinguish it from LVD, both conceptually and technically. We refer the reviewer to our responses to reviewers nu3K, 5vBD and xEDi for a detailed explanation, but we provide a brief summary here for completeness:

1. We incorporate global reasoning using a relative spatial encoding scheme.  
2. We propose a two-branch LVD architecture to learn vertex and keypoint representations jointly.  
3. We present an extension of LVD to the multiview setting.  
4. We introduce $f_k$ to integrate features from off-the-shelf models trained without requiring expensive 3D training data, improving flexibility and efficiency in the pipeline.  
5. We introduce several training strategies that are essential for achieving high-quality reconstructions, as explained in Section 4.2 and in the supplementary material.

---

## Questions

(1-2) In 3D face modeling, the goal can involve various aspects such as reconstructing identity shape, expression, pose, and/or texture. Approaches generally fall into two categories: those that build a face model, such as FLAME [2], and those that learn directly from data to make predictions without relying on an explicit model.

Parametric methods face two main challenges: (1) designing a sufficiently expressive prior that can capture the wide diversity of human faces, and (2) accurately estimating the parameters at inference time. While recent parametric models like FLAME, ImFace [3], or NPHM [4] have become increasingly powerful, improving parameter estimation remains an active area of research for achieving accurate 3D face reconstruction.

Our method does not aim to directly address the representational limitations of 3DMMs. Instead, we focus on the applicability of face reconstruction from RGB inputs in downstream tasks. We propose a model that does not require building an explicit face model, instead directly predicting the 3D vertex positions of the face mesh. This approach preserves the mesh topology while avoiding the constraints when estimating the parameters of the traditional 3DMM, which suffers from mean shape bias.

Our approach is limited by the expressiveness of the training data, which mainly consists of neutral-expression faces. While we do not perform explicit disentanglement, our method preserves mesh topology, allowing a parametric model to be fitted vertex-to-vertex. This enables pose control, animation, or expression editing. For the camera-ready version, we will include additional qualitative results with expressive examples.

(3) The main motivation for including the 3D landmarks branch is to provide global guidance. Both qualitative and quantitative analyses show that this contributes to higher-quality reconstructions. Landmarks offer valuable cues for estimating well-aligned expressions. However, since our focus is on reconstructing subjects with near-neutral expressions, increasing the number of landmarks did not lead to significant improvements in accuracy. As suggested, we present results based on the 68 facial landmarks proposed in [8] that capture expression regions.

| Method     | 3DFAW ↓ |  H3DS ↓ | 
|------------|----------|-----------|
| GLVD  18  | **1.25**    | **1.36**    |
| GLVD  68  | 1.24    | **1.36**    |

(4) A key improvement beyond geometry is obtaining a reliable and realistic texture, as traditional 3DMMs often produce overly smooth and less detailed textures. In GLVD, successfully learning this mapping requires high-quality paired images and meshes to ensure pixel-level alignment. This can be approached in various ways; for instance, methods such as PIFu [5], DiffHuman[6], and DoubleField[7] attempt to regress detailed surface appearance. However, they often produce artifacts and blurry textures. In contrast, methods that predict directly in texture space typically achieve higher visual quality. Introducing a texture branch into LVD is not straightforward and presents significant technical challenges. Making it work effectively would likely require substantial architectural modifications and further investigation. Nonetheless, this line of research is promising and could lead to meaningful progress in achieving realistic 3D human reconstruction.

(5) We agree with the suggestion and will update Figure 2 to label it clearly.

(6) In **HRN**, the authors assume that low-frequency identity and mid-frequency details remain consistent across different views, while lighting, expression, and high-frequency (HF) details are view-dependent. The model explicitly handles pose, lighting, expression, and HF details in a view-dependent manner. The official implementation provides only per-view meshes, which makes it difficult to generate a complete global mesh suitable for evaluation. As a result, we cannot ensure a fair comparison with methods that produce unified, view-consistent reconstructions. Therefore, we use HRN only for single-view comparison.

We quantitatively and qualitatively evaluated **VHAP** on single-view data from the H3DS 2.0 and 3DFAW datasets. While qualitative results cannot be included in the rebuttal, we provide quantitative results demonstrating that GLVD achieves lower reconstruction error and better preserves identity while also being significantly faster:

H3DS 2.0 Dataset:
| Method     | 1 view ↓ |  Time ↓ | 
|------------|----------|-----------|
| VHAP     |  2.15       |  ~200s     |
| GLVD    | **1.36**    | <**1s**    |

3DFAW Dataset:
| Method     | 1 view ↓ | Time↓ | 
|------------|----------|-----------|
| VHAP     | 2.05       | ~200s
| GLVD    | **1.25**       | <**1s**      |

We will extend the evaluation to all multiview configurations and include qualitative comparisons in the camera-ready version.

(7) While we cannot disclose qualitative images, the dataset is well-balanced in terms of gender and includes broad diversity in age and ethnicity across all continents. The raw scans are automatically processed to remove internal mesh faces and non-human elements such as background walls. Each scene is then aligned by registering a template 3D model using non-rigid Iterative Closest Point (ICP). The raw scans are not watertight and often contain large holes, with an overall quality slightly better than that of Microsoft Kinect. Each scan contains approximately 30,000 vertices and 60,000 faces, capturing the full head and shoulders region.

---

Thank you for your constructive and supportive evaluation.  We are pleased that you found the paper well-motivated and conceptually sound.

# Points for Clarification

## Methodological Clarity

(1) The network $g_k(\cdot)$ is a coordinate network, meaning the same shared decoder is applied to all input keypoints. Given an input of shape $18 \times 3$, it outputs a tensor of shape $18 \times 18 \times 3$, from which we extract the diagonal to obtain one displacement per keypoint.

(2) Both $g_v$ and $g_k$ share the same architecture. Each is implemented as an MLP with three linear layers of sizes 1024, 512, and 512, respectively, with ReLU activations and weight normalization applied to each layer. The input is a vector formed by concatenating the 3D coordinates of a point with its corresponding image features, which are obtained by projecting the point onto the image and extracting features via bilinear interpolation. For $g_v$, the 3D point is first transformed into the relative coordinate space $P$, using the estimated 3D keypoints, before being passed to the network. In both cases, the output represents the displacement vector from the input point to each ground-truth target. For keypoint estimation, we use 18 keypoints, and for surface reconstruction, we use 7225 mesh vertices.

(3) We now describe how the optimization is performed during training. The same loss function is used for both branches: keypoints and vertices. In Equation 3 of the main paper, $N$ refers to the number of ground-truth vertices for each training sample, rather than the number of scenes in the dataset (we will update it in the camera ready).

Given a ground-truth mesh $\hat{V} = [\hat{\mathbf{v}}_1, \ldots, \hat{\mathbf{v}}_N]$ and its corresponding image $I$. We randomly sample $M$ 3D points $X = \{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_M\}$, and compute the loss defined in Equation 3 for each of the $M$ points.

$ \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^{M} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N}  \left[ \lambda\_1 \left(            1 - \frac{ \Delta \mathbf{x}_i^j \cdot \hat{\Delta \mathbf{x}}_i^j }{ \| \Delta \mathbf{x}_i^j \|_2 \, \| \hat{\Delta \mathbf{x}}_i^j \|_2 }        \right)   +   \lambda_2 \left| \| \Delta \mathbf{x}_i^j \|_2 - \| \hat{\Delta \mathbf{x}}_i^j \|_2 \right|   \right]$

We train the network to predict the displacement from any point in space to all vertices of the mesh. Therefore, the decoder outputs a tensor of size 18×3 for the landmarks and 7223×3 for the full set of vertices. During training, the loss is averaged across all samples in the batch. We will update and expand the loss description in the camera-ready version.

(4) We will incorporate it to the main text.

(5) While we refer to Figure 2 to illustrate the use of the transformed vertices $P$, we will make this point clearer in Sections 3.4 and 3.5. The transformed vertices are used exclusively in the vertex branch.

---

## Supplementary Material Usage

(1) We pre-train our feature encoder in the task of 3D reconstruction. We represent the surface $\mathcal{S}$ as the zero-level set of a signed distance function $f^{\text{sdf}} : (\mathbf{x}, I) \rightarrow s$, such that $\mathcal{S} = \\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid f^{\text{sdf}}(\mathbf{x}, I) = 0 \\}$. Our goal is to estimate $f^{\text{sdf}}$ through a composition of a feature encoder and a decoder networks. The resulting feature encoder is then used within GLVD. To train on the SDF task, we use non-watertight scans from the same training dataset and minimize $\mathcal{L}\_{\text{Surf}}^{(i)}$ on surface points $N_s$ and $\mathcal{L}\_{\text{Eik}}^{(i)}$ throughout the volume $N_v$:



$ \mathcal{L}\_{\text{Surf}} = \frac{1}{N_s} \sum_{i=0}^{N_s} \left| f\^{\text{sdf}}(\mathbf{x}_i,I) \right| $

$ \mathcal{L}\_{\text{Eik}} = \frac{1}{N_v} \sum_{i=0}^{N_v} \left( \left\| \nabla\_{\mathbf{x}} f^{\text{sdf}}(\mathbf{x}_i,I) \right\|\_2 - 1 \right)^2 $

The loss is averaged over the batch. We will include a detailed explanation in the camera-ready version. The table below (in Minor Remarks) compares the impact of pretraining. Specifically, we evaluate LVD with and without SDF-based pretraining of the feature encoder. Results show that this pretraining is crucial for achieving strong performance in both LVD and GLVD.

(2) For each query point, we predict displacement vectors to all ground-truth vertices for the given scene. At test time, we use the topological index of the query point to update only the corresponding vertex with its predicted displacement. The function $g_k$ operates on 18 3D keypoints. For each query keypoint, it predicts displacement vectors to all 18 target keypoints, resulting in a total of $18 \times 3$ directional components covering the $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes. By repeating this for all 18 keypoints, the final output has a shape of $18 \times 18 \times 3$. However, to obtain the estimated keypoints, we extract the diagonal to obtain one displacement per keypoint.

(3) The initial positions of the 18 query 3D keypoints are randomly sampled within a bounded space. At each iteration, they start from different locations, and through repeated updates, they gradually converge to the final target positions.

---

## Presentation Issues

(1) Our intention is not to directly compare GLVD with optimization-based methods, as their higher computational cost makes the comparison unequal. These methods are included for reference. We agree that bold formatting may be misleading and will revise it in the camera-ready version to follow standard conventions, with a clear caption explaining the grouping.

(2) Our method is applied to a fixed mesh topology throughout the experiments. The phrase “for each mesh” was intended to refer to each training sample using the same template topology. We will revise the wording to clarify this and ensure consistency in the experiments section.
 
(3) We acknowledge the ambiguity in our description and appreciate the reviewer’s observation. The supplementary visualizations correspond to a fixed subset of template vertices.

## LVD vs GLVD

We expand our response here to avoid repeating points already addressed in the Novelty section of our reply to Reviewer 5vBD and xEDi.

We summarize our key improvements below:

1. We incorporate global reasoning using a relative spatial encoding scheme.  
2. We propose a two-branch LVD architecture to learn vertex and keypoint representations jointly.  
3. We present an extension of LVD to the multiview setting.  
4. We introduce $f_k$ to integrate features from off-the-shelf models trained without requiring expensive 3D training data, improving flexibility and efficiency in the pipeline.  
5. We introduce several training strategies that are essential for achieving high-quality reconstructions, as explained in Section 4.2 and in the supplementary material

Two key empirical advantages of GLVD over LVD are its ability to reduce surface artifacts and its increased robustness against collapsed outputs. For a fair comparison, both LVD and GLVD are trained on the same dataset. As shown in Figure 4, LVD produces noticeable artifacts on the face surface, whereas GLVD yields smoother and more stable reconstructions. In Table 2 (a), we report the results of directly applying LVD to the face reconstruction task. When used without modification, LVD yields lower performance compared to the proposed GLVD, highlighting the importance of our architectural and training improvements in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations.

---

## Optimization-based Methods

Optimization-based methods tend to outperform feedforward approaches when sufficient test data is available. However, in highly ill-posed scenarios, typically with a single input image or complex image occlusion, feedforward methods often achieve better results due to their strong learned priors and constrained representation space. GLVD tends to struggle with out-of-distribution test samples, as it relies on patterns seen during training. In contrast, optimization-based methods can adapt more effectively at test time to handle complex or rare cases.

Optimization-based methods are typically orders of magnitude slower and are not directly comparable to feedforward approaches. We highlight this difference in Figure 6. GLVD is inspired by neural field methods commonly used in state-of-the-art avatar reconstruction and adopts a feedforward formulation with an error feedback loop.

To close the performance gap in multiview or less ill-posed scenarios, one could address the limitations in two main ways: by increasing the amount of training data to improve generalization, or by exploring architectural design choices better suited for multiview reconstruction.

Thank you very much for your positive evaluation of our paper. We are glad you found it to be interesting.

---

## Novelty

While there is extensive literature on human mesh recovery (HMR), most methods remain unexplored in other domains such as human face modeling. From the perspective of shape representation, these approaches can be broadly categorized into three groups: parametric body models, volumetric shape models, and vertex-based methods.
In this paper, we build upon the hybrid LVD framework and introduce key design modifications to adapt the vertex-based model for accurate human face modeling. We refer to our response to Reviewer nu3K for a complete discussion of the novelty. 

We summarize our contributions as follows:

- **Keypoint-guided updates**: Introduces a two-branch architecture where 3D keypoints guide vertex refinement.
- **Relative encoding**: Encodes vertices relative to keypoints for pose-aware, view-independent updates.
- **2D priors over 3D supervision**: Uses image features from 2D landmark detector to improve performance without requiring external paired 3D data.
- **Enhanced training**: Improves accuracy through SDF pretraining, noise injection, canonical space, and a proposed loss.

We now address the main differences between KeypointNeRF, LVD, and GLVD:

**KeypointNeRF** learns generalizable neural radiance fields by encoding query points as depth differences relative to 3D keypoints for each view. In the multiview setting, it relies on a neural network to blend view-dependent features. In contrast, GLVD performs a view-independent encoding based on Euclidean distances directly on the 3D vertices, as detailed in Section 3.4. This formulation enables the model to predict vertex displacements relative to the global 3D keypoints, ensuring consistent geometry regardless of the number of input views used to estimate them.

We build upon **LVD**, but our formulation introduces several key differences. LVD lacks explicit modeling of global structure and predicts point trajectories independently, without shared context. To address this, we propose a two-branch architecture: a keypoint branch that estimates global structure and a vertex branch that operates in an encoded 3D space computed from these keypoints at each optimization step.

A simple baseline is to train the function $ f_k(\cdot) $ from scratch and allow the model to learn the proxy 3D landmark representation directly. As shown in Table 3, row (c), this setup yields only minor improvements over LVD. However, incorporating a pretrained 2D landmark detector trained without paired 3D data leads to a significant performance improvement using the same training set. Simply concatenating HRNet features to LVD does not improve results, which highlights the importance of our structural integration and relative encoding.

To make **GLVD** perform effectively, we introduce several modifications to the original LVD framework, as described in Section 4.2. These include pretraining the image feature extractor on a signed distance function task using the same dataset (we refer the reader to our response to Reviewer xEDi), introducing a custom loss over vertex displacements, injecting noise into the predicted keypoints during training to improve robustness, and using a canonical coordinate system in the multiview setting to ensure geometric consistency.

---

## Related Work

Thank you for bringing the papers [1–8] to our attention. While most of them address human mesh recovery, we agree that they are relevant to our work and we will cite and include them in the paper's discussion.

In [1], the authors proposed a three-step approach: (1) selecting landmark points, (2) applying MDS to embed these landmarks in a low-dimensional space, and (3) using distance-based triangulation to embed the remaining points. In GLVD, we adopt a similar strategy by selecting landmarks from facial regions that capture identity-specific information. We then use Euclidean distances to encode mesh vertices relative to these landmarks within the learned space.

Some of the cited references [2–5] primarily target full-body human mesh recovery and remain unexplored in the context of face modeling. These methods often operate in single-image settings [2–5] or on video sequences [7].

**METRO** [2] and **DeFormer** [3] leverage transformer architectures that process mesh joints and vertices jointly as sequences of queries. While differing in attention aggregation strategies, both employ global reasoning via self-attention to capture structural dependencies. However, METRO conditions the model using a global image embedding extracted from a CNN backbone, thereby discarding pixel-aligned spatial detail.

In contrast, **3D Virtual Markers** [4] predicts a set of latent 3D markers and estimates the full mesh as a linear combination of these, effectively collapsing the image into a low-dimensional latent space, similar to traditional 3DMM pipelines. **One-Stage Mesh Recovery** [5] regresses SMPL parameters directly from image features using a transformer. Both approaches are inherently limited by the expressiveness of their low-dimensional latent spaces.

**PyMAF-X** [6] introduces an iterative refinement loop using pixel-aligned features sampled from previous vertex estimates. However, it remains constrained to SMPL parameter regression and does not incorporate explicit landmark or keypoint guidance for structural supervision.

**GART** [7] leverages bones and temporal video input to reconstruct animatable avatars. In contrast, **GLVD** is purely image-driven, requiring neither video nor skeletal priors, and is applicable in monocular and few-shot settings.

Finally, [8] proposes replacing traditional PCA-based 3D face models with convolutional mesh autoencoders for learning facial shape priors. However, this work focuses on latent mesh encoding and does not explore the direct estimation of facial geometry from RGB images, which is central to GLVD.

---

## Questions

(1) We empirically tested various spatial resolutions and found that a feature resolution of 64×64×256 (H, W, C) is sufficient to achieve competitive results. We use this resolution for both branches, although this is not a strict requirement. Our formulation is flexible and can accommodate alternative sources for predicting 3D keypoints. In our experiments, the face occupies most of the image, and we did not observe any noticeable degradation in performance.

We provide detailed network implementation details in the supplementary material. 

(2) In Section 3.4, we introduce $P$, which represents the vertices encoded relative to the keypoints. To compute the next vertex state, we refer to Eq. 1, where the feature map is predicted by $f_v$, and the input vertex $v_i$ corresponds to its encoded representation $P_i$.


---

summary.value: This paper addresses the problem of reconstructing 3D human faces from images. Existing methods mainly fall into two categories: learning-based approaches, which are efficient but often less accurate, and optimization-based approaches, which offer high fidelity but are computationally intensive. The authors propose a hybrid method called Guided Learned Vertex Descent (GLVD), which builds on the Learned Vertex Descent (LVD) framework. GLVD predicts deformations of mesh vertices with a fixed topology of given time step, aiming to combine the accuracy of optimization-based methods with the efficiency of learning-based models. To adapt LVD specifically for face reconstruction, the authors introduce 3D face landmark-based guidance, enhancing the structural coherence of the reconstruction. As a result, their approach achieves state-of-the-art face reconstruction performance while reducing inference time.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
### Strengths

- The paper is clearly written, easy to follow, and well-structured.
- The proposed approach is simple yet effective, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments and detailed ablation studies.
- The authors provide thorough comparisons and clearly show the advantages of their method in both accuracy and efficiency.

### Weaknesses

- The technical novelty beyond LVD feels somewhat limited.
- While the method achieves significant improvements, it does not surpass optimization-based methods in multi-view settings.

questions.value:
1. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, but the technical contribution may appear as a straightforward extension of LVD to face reconstruction. Could you clarify in detail what distinguishes GLVD from simply applying LVD to the face reconstruction task? Specifically, what are the key improvements or advantages?
2. Could the authors provide more analysis or examples of failure cases? In particular, under what conditions does GLVD struggle compared to optimization-based methods? Additionally, could you discuss how to overcome the performance gap in multi-view or less ill-posed scenarios where optimization-based methods perform better?

summary.value: Breaking free from the representational constraints of traditional 3D Morphable Models (3DMMs) is a promising direction in 3D face reconstruction. This paper takes a step in that direction by extending the existing Learned Vertex Descent (LVD) framework—originally designed for human body reconstruction—into the facial domain. The contribution lies in integrating per-vertex neural field optimization with global structural guidance derived from dynamically predicted 3D landmarks.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. Attempting to overcome the representation space limitations of 3DMMs is a promising direction.

2. The paper is easy to follow.

Weaknesses:
1. From the perspective of novelty, the innovation level of this paper seems to fall below the expectations of NeurIPS. Its main framework is based on the Learned Vertex Descent (LVD) framework, and the improvement lies in introducing a face-landmark-based branch similar to LVD. The overall architecture is similar to a dual-path LVD.

2. From the reconstruction results presented in the paper, although it can reconstruct faces of different body types with near-neutral expressions, it seems difficult to reconstruct expression changes such as closed eyes or open mouths (e.g., in the top right corner of Figure 7, the reconstruction fails to capture the closed-eye expression of the male subject).

3. The motivation of the paper is to break through the limitations of 3DMMs, but in terms of shape representation, the reconstructed results appear overly smooth (seemingly unable to reconstruct fine details such as wrinkles or dimples), making it hard to demonstrate superiority over 3DMMs. Additionally, another limitation of 3DMMs is the restricted expression space, and the paper does not show how GLVD addresses expression reconstruction.

4. Please also refer to the “Questions” section.

**AC note:**
I would like to bring to the AC’s attention that Figures 4, 5, and Supplementary Figure 6 in this submission closely resemble Figures 8, 9, and 10 in [1], respectively. I'm unsure whether this level of similarity complies with the conference policy and defer to the AC's judgment. I am unsure whether this situation is acceptable under the conference’s policy.

[1] P. Caselles, E. Ramon, J. García, G. Triginer and F. Moreno-Noguer, "Implicit Shape and Appearance Priors for Few-Shot Full Head Reconstruction," in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, vol. 47, no. 5, pp. 3691-3705, May 2025, doi: 10.1109/TPAMI.2025.3540542.

questions.value:
1. I would like to see more results using GLVD on face images with diverse expressions, as current examples mainly focus on neutral or slightly varied identities.

2. Given the motivation of the paper—overcoming the representation limitations of 3DMMs—this could manifest in two aspects: (1) modeling fine-scale geometry such as wrinkles and dimples, and (2) reconstructing large or micro expression changes. I would be interested in results, theoretical analysis, or discussion from the authors regarding GLVD’s capability in either direction.

3. After reviewing both the main text and supplementary material, it seems that the keypoint selection in the 3D Keypoint Branch does not account for expressive regions, e.g., upper/lower eyelids or mouth lips. Would this limit GLVD’s ability to reconstruct facial expressions accurately?

4. A question for discussion: based on the current dual-branch LVD structure in Figure 2, could the authors consider adding a third “texture LVD” branch to enhance texture reconstruction? This could further address the limited texture representation space of 3DMMs.

5. Figure 2 would benefit from clear labeling of the “3D Keypoint Branch” and “3D Vertex Branch” to improve readability and understanding of the architecture.

6. In Table 1, the method HRN seems to support multi-view reconstruction, but this is not discussed in the paper. Moreover, recent optimization-based methods such as VHAP [2] have also shown the potential to go beyond morphable model priors. 

7. In Lines 199–201, the authors mention employing a proprietary dataset of 10,000 3D head scans. This is a large-scale dataset by the standards of the 3D face community. I am curious about more details of the data, such as mesh resolution (vertex count or face density), scanning quality, and variation.

[2] VHAP: Versatile Head Alignment with Adaptive Appearance Priors

summary.value: This work presents GLVD, a method that builds on top of LVD, by running a sort of dual-scale LVD: First, it estimates a sparse set of keypoints with a LVD pipeline. Then, it uses these keypoints to compute a strong 3D positional encoding signal in canonical space. This signal is used to augment the features for the traditional vertex displacement branch, and improves the results. Whereas LVD was originally applied to a human full-body model and a hand model, GLVD is applied here to a face model, and performs strongly on single-view and multi-view face reconstruction benchmarks.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
## Strengths

- The paper includes an ablation study, which adds credibility to the experimental analysis.  
- It presents strong quantitative results across multiple benchmarks.  
- The proposed approach is well motivated and conceptually sound.  
- A wide range of qualitative results are provided, which help assess the method’s effectiveness.  

---

## Weaknesses and Points for Clarification

### Methodological Clarity

- The method description lacks clarity in several parts, making it difficult to follow without referring to the pipeline figure.
  - For example, in lines 153–154, it is not clear if a separate decoder is used for each keypoint index via the function `g_k`. This should be stated explicitly if true.
  - Similarly, the architecture of `g_v` is not described, making it hard to assess its complexity or design. The same concern applies as for `g_k`.
  - The formulation of the loss in Equation 3 is unclear. It is not specified what the “points” refer to — do they refer to both vertices and keypoints? Also, the loss appears to be summed over all scenes. Does this imply full-batch training rather than stochastic gradient descent? While losses per index are given, the overall objective function is missing. Including it would clarify the learning dynamics, especially if some network components are specific to single keypoints/vertices while others are shared.
  - It appears (after a full read) that the keypoints detected from off-the-shelf heatmaps do not need to correspond to the keypoints used in training. This non-obvious assumption should be stated clearly in the main text.
  - Lines 162–165 introduce an encoding for `P_t`, but its role is never explained in the text.

### Supplementary Material Usage

- Several important details are relegated to the supplementary material without clear indication in the main paper. Either these should be moved to the main text, or the reader should be clearly directed to them.
  - For instance, lines 32–33 of the supplementary state that `f_v` is pre-trained to predict a signed distance function (SDF). This seems like a critical part of training the model. Furthermore, `f_v` is described as a function of the image only — not of a 3D query point — so it's unclear how it is trained to predict an SDF.
  - `g_k` is described as a simple MLP, yet it outputs a tensor of shape `18×18×3` (i.e. more than the actual used output). The rationale for this output shape is not explained.
  - In the supplementary video, certain keypoints appear partway through the sequence. The cause of this behavior could be clarified.

### Presentation Issues

- In Table 1, all results for the proposed method are shown in bold, even though SIRA++ and H3D-Net outperform it in some metrics. This is misleading, as bold font conventionally highlights the best performance in each column. The formatting should be revised to follow this convention. Alternatively, if the intention is to emphasize performance only within a specific subset of methods, this should be explicitly stated, along with a clear justification for excluding SIRA++ and H3D-Net from the comparison.
- In line 176, the phrase “for each mesh” suggests the method is applied to different mesh topologies. However, mesh topology is not discussed in the experiments section.
- Also in line 176, the authors state that a random subset of vertices is selected as target keypoints. However, visualizations in the supplementary material suggest a non-random, possibly handpicked, selection. This inconsistency should be addressed.

---

## Minor Remarks

- Terminology should be made consistent throughout the paper (e.g., "landmarks" vs. "keypoints").
- In line 193, the citation “[52]” seems to refer to the wrong paper. Please verify and correct.
- In lines 106–107, the distinction between “canonical body coordinates” and “face-centric coordinates” is unclear. For instance, PVA [44] appears to rely primarily on pixel-aligned features and positional encoding, not a face-centric coordinate system per se.
- In line 100, citing LVD as a parametric method seems questionable — it may be a stretch.
- The multiview inference aspect of the method deserves more detail and perhaps an ablation study. While not strictly required, this would be a valuable addition.
- Finally, it is unclear why iterations over `g_k` and `g_v` are performed in parallel. An ablation comparing parallel vs. sequential updates (i.e., running all `g_k` steps first) would strengthen the experimental section.

abstract.value: Existing 3D face modeling methods usually depend on 3D Morphable Models, which inherently constrain the representation capacity to fixed shape priors. Optimization-based approaches offer high-quality reconstructions but tend to be computationally expensive. In this work, we introduce GLVD, a hybrid method for 3D face reconstruction from few-shot images that extends Learned Vertex Descent (LVD) by integrating per-vertex neural field optimization with global structural guidance from dynamically predicted 3D keypoints. By incorporating relative spatial encoding, GLVD iteratively refines mesh vertices without requiring dense 3D supervision. This enables expressive and adaptable geometry reconstruction while maintaining computational efficiency. GLVD achieves state-of-the-art performance in single-view settings and remains highly competitive in multi-view scenarios, all while substantially reducing inference time.

TLDR.value: We propose GLVD, a fast and accurate hybrid method for 3D face reconstruction that combines per-vertex neural fields with dynamically predicted 3D landmarks to achieve state-of-the-art quality from just one or a few images.
